column1: Notes: The highest-risk items here are intentional barge-ins, cooperative completions, overlapping speech, and premature endpointing. These directly affect whether the bot understands who owns the floor and whether it captured the user’s full answer.
Over-waiting has a low data score, but it can still be commercially damaging because it increases perceived latency and hang-ups. That impact is not fully captured by these three dimensions.

column4: Failure mode

column3: “I want to book for… um… Wednesday.”
column4: Bot cuts in after “for” or treats “um” as meaningful content.
Bot assumes the user has finished and responds too early.

column4: Bot reprompts too aggressively or times out.

Bot finalizes before full number, ID, address, or card detail is complete.

column2: Long pause with intent to continue
column4: Bot cuts off the answer or starts a repair prompt too early.

column3: User leaves, mutes, or hangs up.
column4: Bot cannot tell if user is thinking, muted, gone, or disconnected.

column1: Notes: The riskiest behavior here is chunked reading, especially for account numbers, claim numbers, addresses, dates, card details, order numbers, and confirmation codes.
A subtle but important distinction: a pause is not always an end-of-turn. Sometimes it means “I am thinking,” “I am reading,” “I am looking something up,” or “I am still holding the floor.”

column3: “The number is 415… actually use my email.”
column4: Bot stores irrelevant partial slot values.

column1: Notes: This is one of the highest-risk categories because the user is explicitly changing their mind or repairing their own speech. A bot that cannot understand repair will often preserve stale or wrong values.
The key rule for this category: later corrected values usually supersede earlier values. For example, in “Tuesday — wait, no, Wednesday,” the business-critical value is Wednesday, not Tuesday.

column1: Notes: These often look lower-risk than slot or intent errors, but they can create severe experience problems when repeated. A single cough is usually recoverable. Constant background noise can destroy the call.
The main failure is not always wrong data. It is often false turn-taking: the bot stops talking, starts listening, or reprompts when no real user turn occurred.

column1: Notes: This category is dangerous because the audio may contain perfectly valid human speech — but not speech intended for the bot.
The critical distinction is:
Speech detected does not mean user-directed instruction detected.
For revenue-touching workflows, the bot must know whether the authorized caller, a helper, a background speaker, or a media source provided the information.

column1: Notes: This category is easy to underestimate because it feels “technical,” not “behavioral.” But in phone production, device and channel behavior directly shape human behavior.
The two highest-risk items here are another IVR/bot and DTMF mishandling. DTMF is especially important because users often assume keypad input is valid in phone systems.

column3: “I don’t want to say that out loud.”

column3: “Sure, because that worked so well last time.”
column4: Bot interprets sarcastic response literally.

Bot misrecognizes speech or responds coldly.

column1: Notes: This category is less about raw ASR and more about conversation judgment.
A frustrated customer may not provide a clean intent like “I want escalation.” They may say:
“This is the third time I’ve called.” “You people keep getting this wrong.” “I already gave you that.” “Can I please talk to someone who can help?”
These are not just emotions. They are often operational signals: repeat contact, failed automation, escalation need, privacy concern, or trust breakdown.

column1: Notes: This category is both a robustness issue and an accessibility issue.

The highest-risk item is persistent recognizer mismatch. If the system consistently fails a speaker because of accent, disability, age, speech rate, or voice quality, the user may have no natural path to correction. They can repeat the same thing many times and still fail.
This is why Correction Risk is high for many rows in this category.

column2: Request for human during sensitive flow
column4: Bot blocks escalation when user is in a high-risk context.

column1: Notes: This is a high-risk category even when the transcript is accurate.
For example, the bot may correctly hear:
“Fine, but don’t record my card number.”
But if it treats that as simple consent, the interpretation is wrong at the policy level. The words were recognized, but the boundary condition was not understood.
The highest-risk rows here are partial consent, sensitive info over-sharing, interrupted disclosures, and blocked escalation during sensitive flows.
